title-group.article-title: Intranasal esketamine plus dexmedetomidine versus dexmedetomidine alone for emergence delirium in pediatric patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Intranasal dexmedetomidine is commonly used preoperatively in pediatric anesthesia to reduce agitation and emergence delirium. Esketamine, with sedative and analgesic ef-fects and minimal respiratory depression at clinical doses, is also widely used in chil-dren. However, current evidence remains limited regarding the efficacy and safety of combining intranasal esketamine with dexmedetomidine versus dexmedetomidine alone in improving cooperation during anesthesia induction and reducing postoperative complications.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This meta-analysis adhered to PRISMA guidelines and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251084757). A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and Wanfang was conducted up to May 25, 2025. The primary outcome included the incidence of emergence delirium, emergence time, mask acceptance score (MAS), parental separation anxiety score (PSAS), and the incidence of adverse events, with pooled effect estimate reported as proportions and relative risk (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Sensitivity analysis were performed to assess the robustness of the results and to identify sources of heterogeneity.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Six studies involving a total of 515 pediatric patients were included. Compared with dexmedetomidine alone, intranasal esketamine combined with dexmedetomidine significantly reduces the incidence of emergence delirium (RR = 0.27, 95% CI: [0.17–0.44], P < 0.00001, I² = 0%). The incidence of bradycardia is also significantly lower in the combination group (RR = 0.24, 95% CI: [0.08–0.72], P = 0.01). No statistically significant differences are observed between the two groups in terms of emergence time or the incidence of nausea and vomiting. The combination group shows lower parental separation anxiety scores and better mask acceptance scores, indicating improved cooperation during anesthesia induction.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Preoperative intranasal administration of esketamine combined with dexmedetomidine significantly reduces the incidence of emergence delirium and bradycardia compared with dexmedetomidine alone.Improved cooperation during anesthesia induction further supports the potential of this combination as a safe and effective alternative to dexmedetomidine monotherapy in pediatric anesthesia.

sec.title: Trial registration
sec.p: Not applicable.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Emergence delirium (ED), first described by Eckenhoff, is a common postoperative central nervous system dysfunction in pediatric patients undergoing general anesthesia, characterized primarily by altered consciousness and behavioral disturbances during the recovery phase [1]. Studies indicate that the incidence of emergence delirium is 63.0% in children under the age of three, compared to 43.0% in those older than three [2]. Due to the immaturity of the central nervous system and incomplete regulation of neurotransmitters, pediatric patients are particularly susceptible to functional brain disturbances under external stimuli such as anesthesia. This susceptibility may result in emergence delirium, characterized by transient agitation, inconsolability, and disorientation. In severe cases, destructive or self-injurious behaviors may occur, including the removal of intravenous lines, urinary catheters, or drainage tubes, thereby complicating perioperative management [3, 4]. These aberrant behaviors may heighten parental anxiety, elevate nursing demands and healthcare costs, and exert lasting effects beyond the immediate recovery period. They are associated with an increased incidence of postoperative maladaptive behaviors in children, which may place additional stress on families and the healthcare system [5].

In international clinical practice, the dexmedetomidine on overall relatively midazolam have better sedation effect and lower the incidence of adverse reactions [6–8], Therefore, it is often used for sedation and perioperative management in children. However, dexmedetomidine still has some dose-related side effects, especially bradycardia and hypotension [9]. A meta-analysis showed that esketamine has the advantages of rapid onset and strong analgesic effect in sedation in children, while its hemodynamic effects are mainly manifested by increased heart rate and blood pressure [10]. Therefore, in clinical practice, dexmedetomidine alone is often difficult to achieve the ideal balance of sedation and hemodynamics. Combined with esketamine, it can enhance the sedative and analgesic effect, and offset the hypotension and bradycardia caused by dexmedetomidine, so as to achieve a more stable sedation state. Esketamine is the s enantiomer of ketamine, which exerts its anesthetic and analgesic effects mainly through non-competitive antagonism with N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors [11]. It has approximately 2-fold receptor affinity for racemic ketamine [12]. Esketamine has rapid onset of sedation and strong analgesic effect in children [10], which is characterized by minimal respiratory depression within the clinical dose range [13]. Although esketamine has shown potential benefits, its use in pediatric anesthesia is still under investigation [13] Current evidence, mainly from studies in adult surgical populations, suggests that esketamine may improve perioperative neurocognitive function [14–16]. This potential neuroprotective effect provides a pharmacological basis for exploring its combination with dexmedetomidine in pediatric anesthesia.

Compared to traditional intramuscular or intravenous administration, intranasal delivery offers a non-invasive route that eliminates the need for venous access, allows for convenient and reliable drug administration, and can be used alone or in combination with other agents. It causes minimal or no tissue damage and is generally well accepted by patients, particularly in pediatric populations or those averse to intravenous injections. Moreover, intranasal administration provides rapid onset and high bioavailability, while avoiding drug degradation in gastrointestinal fluids and bypassing the hepatic first-pass effect [17, 18]. Recent studies have demonstrated that intranasal administration of dexmedetomidine is a practical and effective premedication strategy, providing reliable pre-anesthetic sedation in pediatric general anesthesia [19, 20]. However, it is associated with adverse effects such as bradycardia and hypotension [9]. Combined intranasal administration of esketamine and dexmedetomidine enhances sedative efficacy while reducing the required doses of each agent. This combination also mitigates adverse effects and alleviates postoperative pain in pediatric patients. However, clinical trials investigating the effects of preoperative intranasal administration of esketamine combined with dexmedetomidine, compared to dexmedetomidine alone, on the incidence of emergence delirium in pediatric general anesthesia remain limited. Existing studies are primarily small-sample investigations, and high-quality evidence is still lacking. This study conducts a meta-analysis to evaluate the effects of combined esketamine and dexmedetomidine versus dexmedetomidine alone on the incidence of emergence delirium in pediatric patients undergoing general anesthesia, with the aim of informing clinical practice. To our knowledge, this is the first meta-analysis to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of intranasal esketamine combined with dexmedetomidine versus dexmedetomidine alone in pediatric anesthesia.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This meta-analysis was conducted following the PRISMA guidelines [17], with the protocol prospectively registered in the PROSPERO database (CRD420251084757).

sec.title: Inclusion criteria
sec.p: Studies were included based on the following eligibility criteria: (a) Population: pediatric patients undergoing surgery under general anesthesia; (b)Intervention: preoperative intranasal administration of esketamine combined with dexmedetomidine, with all other perioperative conditions identical to those in the control group; (c)Comparison: preoperative intranasal dexmedetomidine alone, with all other perioperative conditions matched to the intervention group; (d)Study Design: randomized controlled trials (RCTs).

sec.title: Exclusion criteria
sec.p: Studies were excluded if they met any of the following criteria: (a) did not compare intranasal esketamine combined with dexmedetomidine versus dexmedetomidine alone; (b) were non-randomized studies, reviews, case reports, case series, editorials, abstracts, commentaries, letters, expert opinions, or lacked original data; (c) assessed only the individual effects of esketamine or dexmedetomidine rather than their combination; (d) were unpublished or lacked accessible full-text articles; (e) did not provide sufficient data for inclusion in the meta-analysis; (f) reported outcomes that did not meet the objectives of this study.

sec.title: Date sources and searches
sec.p: A comprehensive literature search was performed in six electronic databases—PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and Wanfang—from database inception to May 25, 2025, without restrictions on language or publication status. Search terms included “esketamine,” “delirium,” “randomized controlled trial,” “RCT,” and “random.” Studies were screened manually according to the PICOS framework (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes, and Study design) and restricted to randomized controlled trials. Reference lists of included studies were also examined to identify additional eligible publications. Any discrepancies in study selection were resolved through discussion to ensure accuracy and minimize potential omissions.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: Literature was independently screened by Y.W. and C.L. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or consultation with Y.Wu. as a third reviewer. Duplicate records were removed using EndNote 21 [21]. Initially, titles and abstracts were assessed for relevance based on study design and outcome measures. Full texts of potentially eligible studies were then reviewed for final inclusion.

sec.title: Data extraction
sec.p: Data were extracted by Y.W. and C.L., and independently verified by Y.Wu. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion among the three investigators to ensure accuracy and completeness. The following information is collected from each study: first author, year of publication, country, age of pediatric patients, sample size, type of surgery, and the dosage and route of administration of esketamine and dexmedetomidine in both the intervention and control groups. A summary of the extracted data is presented in Table 1.

sec.p: The primary outcome is the incidence of emergence delirium, defined as a Pediatric Anesthesia Emergence Delirium (PAED) score ≥ 10 [22]. Secondary outcomes include the duration of stay in the postanesthesia care unit (PACU), emergence time, mask acceptance score (MAS) (1 = not afraid, cooperative, easily accepts the mask; 2 = mildly afraid, easily comforted; 3 = moderately afraid, not comforted; 4 = extremely afraid, not comforted), parental separation anxiety score (PSAS) (1 = easily separated; 2 = crying but easily comforted; 3 = crying but not dependent on parents; 4 = crying and dependent on parents), and adverse events, with particular attention to the incidence of bradycardia and nausea/vomiting. The absolute event counts for dichotomous outcomes and the mean ± SD values for continuous outcomes are presented in the corresponding forest plots.

sec.title: Quality assessment
sec.p: Two reviewers independently assessed the risk of bias in the included studies using the Cochrane Collaboration’s Risk of Bias tool [23]. The domains evaluated included: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, selective outcome reporting, and other potential sources of bias. Data entry and analysis were performed using RevMan 5.4 software [24]. In cases of disagreement between the two reviewers, a third reviewer was consulted to reach a consensus.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were conducted using Stata version 18 [25]. Dichotomous outcomes were reported as relative risk (RR) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CI). For continuous outcomes, mean differences (MDs) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated as summary estimates. Heterogeneity across studies was assessed using the Q statistic (Chi-square test), p-values, and the I² statistic [26]. Significant heterogeneity was defined as a p-value ≤ 0.1 or an I² > 50% [27]. A random-effects model was applied regardless of the level of heterogeneity, in consideration of potential clinical and methodological variability across studies. To evaluate the robustness of the results and identify possible sources of heterogeneity, sensitivity analyses were conducted using Stata version 18. As both separation anxiety and mask acceptance are ordinal categorical variables, and all included studies reported outcomes as medians with interquartile ranges (IQR), quantitative synthesis was not feasible. Given the non-normal distribution and non-continuous nature of such data, a structured qualitative review was performed, with study trends summarized using Table 2; Fig. 5. For the outcome of PACU duration, most studies reported data as medians with ranges, while only one study provided means and standard deviations. To improve comparability across studies, the data from that study were converted to estimated medians and ranges using the method described by Wan et al. (2014) [28]. Due to the predominantly skewed or ordinal nature of the data and the lack of individual participant data, a meta-analysis was not performed. Instead, a structured qualitative review (narrative synthesis) was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines [29] and the Cochrane Handbook [30], which recommend narrative synthesis when reliable quantitative pooling is not possible.

sec.title: Search results
sec.p: A total of 531 records were initially identified, of which 295 duplicate entries were removed. After screening titles and abstracts, 213 irrelevant studies were excluded. Following full-text assessment of 23 articles, 6 randomized controlled trials were ultimately included in the analysis (Fig. 1).

caption.p: Flowchart of study selection for the meta-analysis. Flowchart showing the number of studies identified, screened, excluded, and finally included in the meta-analysis.

sec.title: Trial characteristics
sec.p: The studies included pediatric patients undergoing surgery under general anesthesia, with no age restrictions.The basic characteristics of the included studies are summarized in Table 1. The sample sizes range from 58 to 127 participants. Across all six studies [31–36], participants are of comparable age, and the American Society of Anesthesiologists(ASA) Physical Status classifications show minimal variation. In each study, intranasal administration is implemented prior to general anesthesia induction. The dosage of intranasal dexmedetomidine is consistent across studies, administered at either 1 µg/kg or 2 µg/kg. In five studies [31–33, 35, 36], the DS group received low-dose esketamine at 0.5 mg/kg or 1 mg/kg, while one study [34] uses a higher dose of 2 mg/kg. Risk of bias is assessed and presented in Fig. 2. Allocation concealment is reported in four studies [31–34] and is judged to be at low risk of bias. Random sequence generation, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessors, and completeness of outcome data are considered at low risk of bias in all six studies. Although one study [31] used a non-standardized three-point scale for mask acceptance (1 = willingly accepts, 2 = mild resistance, 3 = refuses/requires persuasion), whereas other studies applied a four-point MAS scale (1 = calm/cooperative, 2 = mild fear, 3 = moderate fear, 4 = severe fear/uncooperative), the underlying evaluation logic was comparable across Scales, as both scales assessed the degree of fear or cooperation during mask acceptance. Notably, 1 to 2 points on the 3-point scale, which is comparable to 1 to 2 points on the 4-point scale. Therefore, this variation was considered acceptable and did not substantially affect the consistency of outcome assessment. Consequently, this study was rated as having an unclear risk of bias rather than a high risk. The timing of intranasal administration prior to anesthesia induction varied across the included studies. Three studies [31, 33, 34] reported administration 30 min before induction, one study [36] administered the drug 20 min prior, and another study [35] administered it approximately 35 min before induction. One study [32] did not report the timing of administration. Overall, most studies administered the drug around 30 min before anesthesia induction.

caption.p: Risk of bias assessment. A Risk of bias summary: review authors’ judgments about each risk-of-bias domain for each included study. B Risk of bias graph: review authors’ judgments about each risk-of-bias domain presented as percentages across all included studies

sec.title: Incidence of emergence Delirium, Sensitivity, and subgroup analyses
sec.p: Six randomized controlled trials (n = 515) reported the incidence of emergence delirium (Fig. 3). The random-effects model shows that esketamine combined with dexmedetomidine significantly reduces the risk of emergence delirium compared with dexmedetomidine alone (RR = 0.36, 95% CI [0.16–0.82], P = 0.02), although substantial heterogeneity exists among studies (I² = 72.9%) (Fig. 3A). To assess the robustness of the results, a leave-one-out sensitivity analysis is performed (Fig. 3B). The results indicate that sequential omission of any study yields pooled RRs between 0.27 and 0.42, suggesting that the overall effect direction remains consistent. However, exclusion of either Liao 2024 or Lu 2021 slightly increases the upper limit of the 95% CI above 1, indicating that statistical significance is partly influenced by individual studies. Notably, omitting Zhang 2025 markedly reduces heterogeneity (I² = 0%), with a pooled RR of 0.27 (95% CI [0.17–0.44], P < 0.00001), and the confidence interval becomes substantially narrower (Fig. 3B). Based on these findings, a subgroup analysis according to esketamine dose (0.5 mg/kg, 1 mg/kg, and 2 mg/kg) is conducted (Fig. 3C), resulting in markedly reduced within-subgroup heterogeneity. In the 0.5 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg subgroups, combination therapy significantly reduces the incidence of emergence delirium, with I² = 0% within each subgroup. In the 2 mg/kg subgroup, which includes only Zhang 2025, no statistically significant difference is observed between combination therapy and dexmedetomidine alone.

caption.p: Forest plot of the incidence of emergence delirium. A Forest plot showing the effect sizes for the incidence of emergence delirium in all included studies. B Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis for the effect size of the incidence of emergence delirium. C Subgroup analysis was performed according to dose. CI: confidence interval; RR: risk ratio

sec.title: Emergence time and incidence of bradycardia and nausea/vomiting
sec.p: Three studies (n = 240) compare emergence time between the esketamine plus dexmedetomidine group and the dexmedetomidine-only group. No heterogeneity is observed among studies (I² = 0%). The pooled analysis shows no statistically significant difference in emergence time between groups (MD = − 0.65, 95% CI: [–1.32, 0.02], P = 0.06) (Fig. 4A).Four studies (n = 368) assess the incidence of bradycardia between the two groups. No heterogeneity is detected (I² = 0%). The combined results indicate that the esketamine plus dexmedetomidine group has a significantly lower incidence of bradycardia compared to dexmedetomidine alone (RR = 0.24, 95% CI: [0.08, 0.72], P = 0.01) (Fig. 4B).Four studies [32, 33, 35, 36] (n = 299) evaluate the incidence of nausea and vomiting. No heterogeneity is found (I² = 0%). The pooled analysis shows no significant difference in the incidence of nausea and vomiting between groups (RR = 1.55, 95% CI: [0.50, 4.83], P = 0.45) (Fig. 4C).

B Forest plot showing the effect sizes for the incidence of bradycardia. C Forest plot showing the effect sizes for the incidence of nausea and vomiting. sec.title: Separation anxiety, mask acceptance, and PACU time
sec.p: Five studies (n = 441) compare preoperative separation anxiety scores between the two groups. As the data are reported as medians with interquartile ranges, a meta-analysis is not conducted. Instead, a qualitative synthesis is performed. As shown in Table 2; Fig. 5A, the combination group exhibits lower anxiety scores during child–parent separation, suggesting a potential advantage in alleviating separation anxiety.Five studies (n = 457) report differences in mask acceptance scores. Due to the use of median and IQR data across all studies, traditional meta-analysis is not feasible; therefore, a qualitative analysis is conducted. As demonstrated in Table 2; Fig. 5B, children in the combination group tended to exhibit better mask acceptance, suggesting potentially higher cooperation compared with the control group. Five studies (n = 457) provide PACU recovery time data for both groups. Since most studies report medians, suggesting a skewed distribution, a meta-analysis is not performed. Instead, a structured narrative synthesis is used for comparison. As illustrated in Table 2; Fig. 5C, PACU time was largely similar between groups; four studies reported slightly shorter times with the combination, whereas one reported a slightly longer time.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Emergence delirium (ED) is a frequent cognitive disturbance observed during recovery after pediatric general anesthesia. It manifests as postoperative agitation, confusion, and motor restlessness. Although self-limiting, ED may lead to self-injury, accidental extubation, prolonged post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) stay, and potentially adverse long-term behavioral effects. The incidence of ED ranges widely from 10% to 80% [37]. ED and emergence agitation (EA), although frequently used interchangeably in the literature, represent two conceptually distinct postoperative phenomena [38]. ED is characterized by a disturbance in awareness and cognition with disorientation and perceptual alterations [1], whereas EA refers to agitation despite preserved consciousness and orientation [39]. This distinction is clinically important, as ED and EA differ in presentation, underlying mechanisms, and therapeutic strategies. In the present meta-analysis, all included trials assessed ED using the PAED scale, which was specifically developed and validated for the diagnosis of ED rather than EA [22]. Therefore, our pooled findings predominantly reflect ED rather than EA. Future randomized trials are encouraged to clearly distinguish ED from EA when defining endpoints, selecting assessment tools, and interpreting postoperative behavioral outcomes. The pathogenesis of ED is considered multifactorial, involving volatile anaesthetics, surgery type, age, parental anxiety, patient anxiety, pre-existing behaviours and interactions with health-care providers [40]. Given its significant impact on recovery quality and anesthesia satisfaction, prevention and intervention strategies are helpful in pediatric anesthesia management.

In the sensitivity analysis, Zhang 2025 is observed to have a significant impact on overall heterogeneity. Unlike the 0.5–1 mg/kg esketamine doses used in the other studies, this study administered a higher dose of 2 mg/kg. Previous studies indicate that ketamine and its S-enantiomer may exert differential central nervous system effects at different dose levels, and higher doses may attenuate or even counteract potential benefits in preventing emergence delirium [41, 42]. Therefore, this dose difference may constitute an important source of clinical and methodological heterogeneity, making it difficult to directly pool the effects of high-dose studies with those of low-to-moderate dose studies. Based on these observations, a subgroup analysis according to esketamine dose is conducted. Although heterogeneity within each subgroup is markedly reduced after stratification, these results should be interpreted with caution. Notably, the 0.5 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg subgroups each include only two studies, while the 2 mg/kg subgroup includes only Zhang 2025. With such a small number of included studies, the I² statistic has limited power to detect heterogeneity; therefore, I² = 0% does not necessarily indicate the absence of between-study differences. These findings suggest that the current subgroup analysis primarily reflects an exploratory trend rather than a definitive dose–effect relationship. Overall, the results indicate that the effect of esketamine in preventing emergence delirium may be dose-dependent, with low-to-moderate doses combined with dexmedetomidine potentially offering greater benefit, but further high-quality, dose-comparable randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these observations. Previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses have demonstrated that intranasal dexmedetomidine has been associated with improved postoperative agitation and delir-ium scores, while low-dose esketamine reduces emergence delirium (ED) without pro-longing PACU stay or increasing postoperative nausea and vomiting [41, 43, 44].From a pharmacological perspective, esketamine attenuates central nervous system hyperexcitability by inhibiting glutamate-mediated NMDA receptor activation, thereby reducing the likelihood of ED [45, 46]. These findings are consistent with the present results and align with previous studies. However, it should be noted that Chen S et al. [47] report an increased risk of ED when esketamine is administered at near-anesthetic doses, highlighting that dosage and route of administration are helpful determinants of its safety profile. Future studies are warranted to further clarify the risk–benefit balance of various dosing regimens.

Notably, this study also systematically evaluates several secondary outcomes. In terms of cardiovascular events, the incidence of bradycardia is significantly lower in the combination group compared to the dexmedetomidine-only group (RR = 0.24, 95% CI: [0.08–0.72], P = 0.01). Bradycardia can reduce cerebral blood flow and oxygen delivery, and in severe cases may contribute to hypoxemia and metabolic acidosis [48]. While dexmedetomidine, as an α2-adrenoceptor agonist, provides effective sedation, it is associated with a dose-dependent risk of bradycardia, especially in children [9, 49]. Esketamine, a non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist, stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, resulting in increased heart rate and blood pressure [50]. This sympathetic activation may counteract the adverse cardiovascular effects of dexmedetomidine. Therefore, the combination therapy offers a more favorable balance between sedation and hemodynamic stability.

Secondly, sedation quality and anesthesia induction are evaluated using the Preoperative Separation Anxiety Score (PSAS) and the Mask Acceptance Score (MAS). Children frequently experience separation anxiety before surgery, often manifesting as resistance, crying, and avoidance behaviors. These reactions increase the difficulty of anesthesia induction and may lead to intraoperative agitation and postoperative behavioral disturbances. Pharmacologic interventions aimed at alleviating anxiety can facilitate smoother parental separation and improve perioperative outcomes [51]. The meta-analysis results showed that the combined group had lower PSAS scores and better MAS scores, suggesting that the combined group tended to have better cooperation during parental separation and mask induction. Similarly, Jiwei et al. [52] report that intranasal esketamine administration before surgery in children with congenital heart disease results in reduced separation anxiety, higher parental satisfaction, and better mask acceptance. These findings are clinically relevant, as separation difficulties heighten parental anxiety and prolong preoperative preparation time, while poor induction can lead to patient movement, induction failure, or airway complications, thereby interfering with the anesthesia plan. The rapid onset and mild dissociative sedative properties of esketamine may be key mechanisms in reducing preoperative anxiety and improving cooperation, particularly in children with pronounced surgical fear.

No significant difference in emergence time was found between groups, though a trend toward shorter recovery was observed with combined treatment. Based on existing literature, the reduction in the incidence of emergence delirium may itself be associated with a smoother emergence process, which could indirectly contribute to a shorter recovery time [53]. Regarding PACU recovery time, a qualitative synthesis was performed due to the skewed distribution of data and the widespread use of medians with interquartile ranges. Across the included studies, PACU duration was generally similar between the combination group and the dexmedetomidine-alone group, with most studies reporting slightly shorter recovery times following combined administration. These results suggest that the combination group does not appear to delay postoperative recovery or prolong PACU length of stay. From a clinical perspective, maintaining comparable recovery times while reducing emergence delirium and improving induction cooperation may enhance the overall perioperative management of pediatric patients.

Regarding postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), no significant increase in incidence was found in the combined group, indicating good safety and tolerability while improving emergence quality. This is particularly important for high-risk pediatric populations (e.g., those with prior PONV or undergoing tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy), where appropriate dosing can achieve optimal sedation and analgesia safely.

However, limitations exist. The number of included studies is small; some secondary outcomes such as hypotension, induction failure, and patient movement were reported infrequently with variable definitions, potentially affecting pooled accuracy. In addition, most studies were single-center with small sample sizes and were geo-graphically concentrated in China, where patient populations, anesthesia practices, peri-operative management, and cultural factors influencing pediatric anxiety and behavior may differ from those in other regions. This geographic concentration may limit the generalizability of the findings and introduce potential publication bias. Therefore, the conclusions should be interpreted with caution. Future large-scale, multicenter, high-quality international randomized controlled trials are warranted to further validate the safety and efficacy of this combined regimen across different surgical settings and pediatric subgroups.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In conclusion, this meta-analysis demonstrates that preoperative intranasal esketamine combined with dexmedetomidine in pediatric elective surgery is associated with a significant reduction in emergence delirium and bradycardia, without an increased risk of common adverse events such as nausea and vomiting. In addition, qualitative synthesis suggested that this combination tended to improve preoperative anxiety and induction cooperation. These findings derived from ordinal and non-normally distributed outcomes should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory, and warrant further investigation in well-designed randomized trials.

These findings underscore the multidimensional benefits of this regimen in optimizing anesthesia quality and enhancing perioperative safety and experience in children. Compared to most single-agent interventions, this study highlights the dual goals of “synergistic sedation”, enhancing its clinical applicability.
